lines.text: The endless steppe, the first riders of horses, Silk Road towns, Soviet rockets and a nation reborn. This is the story of Kazakhstan.
When the last ice age ended, the Aral Sea filled to become one of the largest lakes on Earth. Its story would end in tragedy.
More than five thousand years ago, the Botai people of the northern steppe were among the first to tame horses.
In 751, by the Talas River, a Tang Chinese army met the Abbasids. Tradition says the art of papermaking passed west afterwards.
In the thirteenth century the Mongols came, and the Golden Horde ruled the western steppes for more than two centuries.
In the town of Turkistan, the conqueror Timur raised a great shrine to a Sufi poet, left unfinished to this day.
In the fifteenth century the Kazakh nomads formed their own khanate, later split into three hordes.
In 1830 a small fort was founded on the northern steppe. Much later, as Astana, it would become the capital.
Abai, a poet and thinker born in 1845, would found written Kazakh literature, as the Russian empire took hold of the steppe.
In 1854 the Russians founded a fort beneath the Tian Shan mountains, which grew into Almaty, the largest city.
Under Soviet rule, forced collectivisation brought a terrible famine that killed more than a third of the Kazakh people.
In 1940 Nursultan Nazarbayev was born. He would rule independent Kazakhstan for almost thirty years.
From 1949 the Soviets tested their nuclear bombs at Semipalatinsk, some four hundred and fifty explosions in all.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, born in 1953, would succeed Nazarbayev as president.
In 1955 the Soviets began building Baikonur on the steppe, the world's first spaceport, which would launch Sputnik.
From there in the spring of 1961, Yuri Gagarin rode Vostok One around the Earth, the first human in space.
Gennady Golovkin, born in 1982, would become a middleweight boxing champion known around the world as Triple G.
In December 1986, young Kazakhs rioted in Almaty against a Russian party boss, an early sign that Soviet rule was cracking.
In 1991 the Soviet Union fell apart, and Kazakhstan, the largest landlocked country in the world, became independent.
In 2000 a giant oil field, Kashagan, was found beneath the Caspian Sea, one of the largest finds in decades.
In the new capital Astana, the Bayterek Tower rose, shaped like a golden egg held in a tree.
In January 2022, protests over fuel prices turned into deadly unrest across the country.
From the first horse riders to a capital of glass, the steppe still shapes Kazakhstan's story.
